Peacenik
PEES-nik
noun (Boomer slang)
Peace + the Yiddish/Russian suffix -nik (one who is connected with something), which entered American English with Sputnik (1957) and beatnik (coined by San Francisco columnist Herb Caen, 1958). Peacenik appears by 1963 as a mildly mocking name for anti-war and anti-nuclear demonstrators, and became common during the Vietnam protests. Opponents used it as a jab; many protesters wore it as a badge.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A peacenik was an anti-war activist of the 1960s and 70s — marching against the bomb, against Vietnam, against the draft — usually said with a smirk by those who thought him naive or disloyal. The Christian observation: the word mocks something the Lord Jesus blessed, and it also exposes something the movement lacked. Our Lord said, "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Mat 5:9). The believer is commanded, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (Rom 12:18), and Isaiah’s vision of swords beaten into plowshares (Isa 2:4) is engraved on the wall of the United Nations because it is the deepest hope of every honest heart. So a Christian ought never to sneer at the longing for peace. But Scripture is not pacifist in the way many peaceniks were. It knows "a time of war, and a time of peace" (Ecc 3:8); it gives the magistrate the sword; and it warns against the prophets who cry "Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14). Isaiah’s plowshares come only when the LORD Himself shall "judge among the nations" (Isa 2:4). The peacemaker Christ blessed is not the one who refuses every conflict but the one who brings men to the reconciliation His blood purchased — first with God, then with one another.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer slang (by 1963) for an anti-war activist, often derisive — a longing Christ blessed in the peacemakers (Mat 5:9), but which Scripture roots in reconciliation with God, not the mere absence of war.

expand to see more

PEACENIK, n. (Boomer slang, by 1963; often derisive) An anti-war or anti-nuclear activist; a pacifist demonstrator. "A bunch of peaceniks were picketing the recruiting office."

Webster (1828) — PEACE, noun [Latin pax, paco, to appease.] 1. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation; applicable to society, to individuals, or to the temper of the mind. 2. Freedom from war with a foreign nation; public quiet. 3. Freedom from internal commotion or civil war. 4. Freedom from private quarrels, suits or disturbance.

Formed on the pattern of beatnik (1958) and Sputnik (1957); compare refusenik, no-goodnik.

Decode for families: the word was a sneer. The Christian may disagree with a protester’s politics without sneering at his desire for peace.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:9 — "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."

Rom 12:18 — "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."

Isa 2:4 — "And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more."

Ecc 3:8 — "A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace."

Jer 6:14 — "They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace."

Modern Corruption

The word mocked the longing for peace, and the movement often made peace an end in itself; Scripture blesses peacemakers but grounds peace in the judgment and reconciliation of God, not in disarmament alone.

expand to see more

There are two corruptions here, one on each side of the picket line. The first belongs to the mockers. They made a joke of a hope the prophets held sacred, and in doing so they implied that the desire for peace is weakness. Our Lord blessed it (Mat 5:9). A Christian father should teach his son to honor the desire even when he disputes the policy.

The second belongs to the movement itself. Much of the peace movement believed that peace is simply the absence of war, achievable by marching and disarmament, and that the warrior is always the villain. Scripture knows better. There is "a time of war, and a time of peace" (Ecc 3:8), and the false prophets of Jeremiah’s day were precisely the ones who cried "Peace, peace" when judgment was at the gate (Jer 6:14). The plowshares of Isaiah 2:4 are the fruit of the LORD’s own judging and rebuking of the nations. Peace is not the first thing; it is the fruit of righteousness. The true peacemaker carries the gospel of the One who "made peace through the blood of his cross" — and that peace, once made with God, goes on to make peace between men.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French pais, Latin pax → English peace + Yiddish / Slavic -nik (via Sputnik 1957, beatnik 1958) → peacenik, by 1963.

expand to see more

Latin pax, pacis — a compact, an agreement, peace

Hebrew shalom — wholeness, well-being, peace with God and man

Yiddish / Slavic agent suffix -nik — one associated with a thing

1957–58: Sputnik, beatnik popularize -nik in American slang

By 1963: peacenik, often derisive, for anti-war and anti-nuclear demonstrators

Usage

""Uncle Ray called them peaceniks; Aunt Carol marched with them.""

"Blessed are the peacemakers (Mat 5:9) — but peace with God comes before peace on the picket line."

"Beware the cry of "Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14)."
